title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect
text:
1 Understand the tools and databases
NCBI Entrez Direct (EDirect) is a collection of programs that search and retrieve records from the Entrez databases. Four programs do most of the work in this tutorial:







Program
Role in a data pipeline




esearch
Search a database and pass its result set downstream.


epost
Post a saved list of identifiers or accessions for downstream use.


efetch
Retrieve records in a requested format.


xtract
Select fields from XML and write tabular text.



The EDirect Cookbook collects reusable shell recipes. The examples here use the same search-fetch- extract grammar, expressed through Julia’s process-pipeline interface so that they run at the Julia REPL.
Two Entrez databases have different jobs:

taxonomy resolves names, ranks, identifiers, and descendants;
nuccore searches nucleotide records from sources including GenBank and RefSeq.

A Taxonomy ID identifies an organism or named group. A nucleotide accession identifies a sequence record. Do not substitute one for the other.

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect from Julia
text:
1 Install EDirect
NCBI Entrez Direct (EDirect) provides programs for searching and retrieving records from the Entrez databases. EDirect requires a Unix-compatible shell. On Windows, use Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).
Run the installer from the system shell:
$ sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/entrezdirect/install-edirect.sh)"
The $ marks the shell prompt and is not part of the command. The installer places EDirect in ~/edirect and offers to add that directory to PATH. Accept the offer, then restart the terminal if instructed.
Confirm that the shell finds each program used below:
$ command -v esearch epost efetch xtract
/home/student/edirect/esearch
/home/student/edirect/epost
/home/student/edirect/efetch
/home/student/edirect/xtract

$ esearch -version
26.2
The path contains the local user name. The version may be newer than the one shown here. The EDirect release notes document version changes.
Create a project directory and start Julia with a project environment:
$ mkdir -p bear-edirect-project
$ cd bear-edirect-project
$ julia --project=.
Add DataFrames.jl from Julia’s package mode:
julia> ]

pkg> add DataFrames
Press Backspace at an empty pkg> prompt to return to julia>.
Load the required names and create the raw-data directory:
julia> using DataFrames: DataFrame, leftjoin, nrow, select, unstack

julia> import Dates

julia> raw_dir = joinpath("data", "raw")
"data/raw"

julia> mkpath(raw_dir)
"data/raw"

julia> pwd()
"/home/student/bear-edirect-project"

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect
text:
3 Prepare a small project
Create a dedicated working directory and start Julia with a project environment:
$ mkdir -p bear-edirect-project/data/raw
$ cd bear-edirect-project
$ julia --project=.
The remainder of the workflow runs at julia>. Verify the working directory and confirm that Julia can locate EDirect:
julia> pwd()
"/home/student/bear-edirect-project"

julia> Sys.which("esearch")
"/home/student/edirect/esearch"

julia> readchomp(`esearch -version`)
"26.2"
If Sys.which("esearch") returns nothing, exit Julia, correct the PATH in the terminal, and restart Julia before continuing.
Install DataFrames.jl in this project for the marker-availability table:
julia> ]

pkg> add DataFrames
Press ] at an empty Julia prompt to enter package mode. Press Backspace at an empty package prompt to return to julia>.

3.1 Define a reusable pipeline writer
Julia represents an external command with backticks and connects commands with pipeline. Define a small helper that writes the last command’s output to a file:
julia> function save_pipeline(
           destination::AbstractString,
           commands::Cmd...;
           append::Bool = false,
       )::Nothing
           mode = append ? "a" : "w"
           open(destination, mode) do output
               command_pipeline = pipeline(commands...)
               run(pipeline(command_pipeline; stdout = output))
           end
           return nothing
       end
save_pipeline (generic function with 1 method)
The default append = false opens the destination with mode "w": rerunning a query replaces that result file. Passing append = true uses mode "a" and adds output at the end. We will use both behaviors deliberately.







NoteWhy not type a vertical bar after shell>



EDirect documentation normally shows Unix pipelines with |. Julia’s REPL shell mode can launch individual commands, but it does not give | the same meaning as a Unix shell pipeline. Julia’s pipeline(command1, command2) is the REPL-native equivalent and avoids another layer of shell quoting.

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect
section: 4 Resolve biological concepts with NCBI Taxonomy
text:
4 Resolve biological concepts with NCBI Taxonomy
Common-language groups are not sufficiently precise database targets. For example, “bears” might include fossils, subspecies, environmental samples, or records identified only to genus. The NCBI Taxonomy Browser accepts common or scientific names and shows the accepted name, rank, lineage, and Taxonomy ID.
Use the browser to resolve the concept bears. The current record is Ursidae, Taxonomy ID 9632, at the rank family. Its descendants include extant species, fossil species, subspecies, and incompletely identified records, so Ursidae alone is too broad for our terminal taxa.
The exact Entrez query is:
txid9632[subtree] AND species[rank] AND specified[prop] NOT extinct[prop]
Its parts make the biological target explicit:







Query term
Meaning




txid9632[subtree]
Ursidae and every descendant below it.


species[rank]
Keep records whose NCBI rank is species.


specified[prop]
Exclude incompletely identified taxa such as Ursus sp..


NOT extinct[prop]
Exclude taxa marked extinct in NCBI Taxonomy.



Taxonomy is a curated classification and identifier system for organizing NCBI records. It is not an authoritative nomenclatural source or a phylogenetic hypothesis; NCBI itself directs researchers to the relevant systematic literature for those purposes. The Taxonomy documentation explains its scope, and the browser displays this limitation on individual taxon pages.

4.1 Search for extant bear species
Search Taxonomy, fetch the matched XML records, and extract 3 fields:
julia> bear_query =
           "txid9632[subtree] AND species[rank] AND specified[prop] NOT extinct[prop]";

julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/bear-taxa.tsv",
           `esearch -db taxonomy -query $bear_query`,
           `efetch -format xml`,
           `xtract -pattern Taxon -element TaxId ScientificName Rank`,
       )

julia> print(read("data/raw/bear-taxa.tsv", String))
9634    Helarctos malayanus species
9636    Melursus ursinus    species
9638    Tremarctos ornatus  species
9642    Ursus thibetanus    species
9643    Ursus americanus    species
9644    Ursus arctos    species
9646    Ailuropoda melanoleuca  species
29073   Ursus maritimus species
NCBI databases change. Treat 8 species as a checkpoint for this worked example, not as a promise that every future run has the same rows or row order. Stop and investigate if your result differs before retrieving sequences.
Parse the table in Julia and save a plain Taxonomy-ID manifest:
julia> bear_taxon_rows = split.(readlines("data/raw/bear-taxa.tsv"), '\t');

julia> bear_taxids = getindex.(bear_taxon_rows, 1);

julia> bear_taxa = getindex.(bear_taxon_rows, 2);

julia> length(bear_taxa)
8

julia> write(
           "data/raw/bear-taxids.txt",
           join(bear_taxids, '\n') * "\n",
       );
This is the simple one-query pattern: 1 query produced 1 result table, from which we saved its identifiers.


4.2 Transfer the method to shark families
The common term sharks is especially useful for exposing a naming trap. Chondrichthyes includes cartilaginous fishes, and Elasmobranchii includes both sharks and rays. In the current NCBI classification, the intended group is Selachii. The Taxonomy Browser tree makes those inclusions visible.
First resolve the exact current Selachii record rather than guessing its ID:
julia> selachii_query = "\"Selachii\"[Scientific Name]";

julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/selachii-taxon.tsv",
           `esearch -db taxonomy -query $selachii_query`,
           `efetch -format xml`,
           `xtract -pattern Taxon -element TaxId ScientificName Rank`,
       )

julia> print(read("data/raw/selachii-taxon.tsv", String))
Inspect that single row. Then use its returned Taxonomy ID to find every currently represented, specified, non-extinct family below it:
julia> selachii_fields = split(readline("data/raw/selachii-taxon.tsv"), '\t');

julia> selachii_taxid = selachii_fields[1];

julia> shark_family_query =
           "txid$(selachii_taxid)[subtree] AND family[rank] " *
           "AND specified[prop] NOT extinct[prop]";

julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/shark-families.tsv",
           `esearch -db taxonomy -query $shark_family_query`,
           `efetch -format xml`,
           `xtract -pattern Taxon -element TaxId ScientificName Rank`,
       )

julia> shark_family_rows = readlines("data/raw/shark-families.tsv");

julia> length(shark_family_rows)

julia> foreach(println, shark_family_rows)
The count is intentionally not printed in this text: this query asks a live database, and a changing result is itself information to record. Save the query next to the result:
julia> write(
           "data/raw/shark-family-query.txt",
           shark_family_query * "\n",
       );

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect from Julia
text:
4 Combine identifiers from multiple queries
Separate searches express a sampling design that names independent targets rather than 1 taxonomic subtree.

4.1 Save separate results and combine them
Specify 1 representative for each of 3 mammal orders:
julia> mammal_targets = DataFrame(
           order = ["Primates", "Rodentia", "Artiodactyla"],
           scientific_name = [
               "Homo sapiens",
               "Mus musculus",
               "Bos taurus",
           ],
           file_stem = ["primates", "rodents", "artiodactyls"],
       );

julia> mammal_queries = [
           "\"$(name)\"[Scientific Name]"
           for name in mammal_targets.scientific_name
       ];
Run each esearch invocation, then pass each captured result to a separate efetch invocation:
julia> mammal_search_results = [
           read(`esearch -db taxonomy -query $query`, String)
           for query in mammal_queries
       ];

julia> mammal_uid_texts = [
           read(
               pipeline(
                   `efetch -format uid`;
                   stdin = IOBuffer(search_xml),
               ),
               String,
           )
           for search_xml in mammal_search_results
       ];

julia> mammal_targets.taxid = parse.(Int, strip.(mammal_uid_texts));

julia> select(mammal_targets, :order, :scientific_name, :taxid)
3×3 DataFrame
 Row │ order          scientific_name  taxid
     │ String         String           Int64
─────┼────────────────────────────────────────
   1 │ Primates       Homo sapiens       9606
   2 │ Rodentia       Mus musculus      10090
   3 │ Artiodactyla   Bos taurus         9913
Write 1 identifier file per query:
julia> mammal_id_paths = [
           joinpath(raw_dir, "$(stem)-taxid.txt")
           for stem in mammal_targets.file_stem
       ];

julia> write.(mammal_id_paths, mammal_uid_texts);

julia> readlines.(mammal_id_paths)
3-element Vector{Vector{String}}:
 ["9606"]
 ["10090"]
 ["9913"]
Read the separate files, concatenate their rows, and write the combined file:
julia> combined_mammal_taxids = reduce(vcat, readlines.(mammal_id_paths))
3-element Vector{String}:
 "9606"
 "10090"
 "9913"

julia> write(
           joinpath(raw_dir, "mammal-representative-taxids.txt"),
           join(combined_mammal_taxids, '\n') * "\n",
       );


4.2 Append repeated query results
Open a fresh destination and append each captured efetch result to its IOStream:
julia> appended_path = joinpath(
           raw_dir,
           "mammal-representative-taxids-appended.txt",
       );

julia> open(appended_path, "w") do output
           for query in mammal_queries
               search_xml = read(
                   `esearch -db taxonomy -query $query`,
                   String,
               )
               uid_text = read(
                   pipeline(
                       `efetch -format uid`;
                       stdin = IOBuffer(search_xml),
                   ),
                   String,
               )
               write(output, uid_text)
           end
       end;

julia> @assert readlines(appended_path) == combined_mammal_taxids
Opening the destination with "w" replaces any previous content before the loop begins. Opening the file separately with "a" would retain old content and duplicate identifiers when the cell is rerun.

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect
text:
6 Query sequence-record availability
Taxonomic coverage does not imply molecular-marker coverage. Search the nuccore database separately for every taxon-marker combination. This example compares 2 mitochondrial markers, CYTB and COX1, with the nuclear marker RAG1.
The Nucleotide query
txid29073[ORGN:noexp] AND CYTB[GENE]
means that the record is indexed directly to Ursus maritimus, rather than a descendant taxon, and has CYTB in the gene field. An ordinary ORGN search expands through descendants; ORGN:noexp prevents that expansion. See the EDirect manual’s search examples and use einfo -db nuccore -fields when you need to inspect available fields.
Define a function that returns the live search count:
julia> using DataFrames: DataFrame, unstack

julia> function count_nuccore_records(
           taxid::AbstractString,
           marker::AbstractString,
       )::Int
           query = "txid$(taxid)[ORGN:noexp] AND $(marker)[GENE]"
           count_text = read(
               pipeline(
                   `esearch -db nuccore -query $query`,
                   `xtract -pattern ENTREZ_DIRECT -element Count`,
               ),
               String,
           )
           sleep(0.4)
           return parse(Int, strip(count_text))
       end
count_nuccore_records (generic function with 1 method)
The short pause keeps this small loop below NCBI’s unauthenticated request-rate limit. Do not parallelize these searches. NCBI’s E-utilities usage guidelines also recommend batching large retrievals rather than issuing one request for every record.
Build a long table, one observation per taxon-marker pair:
julia> markers = ["CYTB", "COX1", "RAG1"];

julia> marker_counts = DataFrame(
           taxon = String[],
           marker = String[],
           record_count = Int[],
       );

julia> for (taxid, taxon) in zip(bear_taxids, bear_taxa), marker in markers
           record_count = count_nuccore_records(taxid, marker)
           push!(marker_counts, (taxon, marker, record_count))
       end

julia> marker_counts
Reshape it into the requested taxon-by-marker matrix:
julia> marker_matrix = unstack(
           marker_counts,
           :taxon,
           :marker,
           :record_count,
       );

julia> sort!(marker_matrix, :taxon)

julia> marker_matrix
Save the observed counts as a TSV without adding another package:
julia> open("data/raw/bear-marker-counts.tsv", "w") do output
           println(output, join(names(marker_matrix), '\t'))
           for row in eachrow(marker_matrix)
               println(output, join(string.(collect(row)), '\t'))
           end
       end







WarningA record count is a screening variable



A large count does not establish orthology, completeness, correct identification, sequence quality, or independence among records. A count of 0 can also reflect a gene-name synonym or missing annotation. Use the matrix to identify candidates, then inspect record metadata and biological comparability.

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect
text:
7 Inspect candidates before selecting records
Start with a narrow single-taxon query for complete mitochondrial CYTB records of a plausible length. This is the simple one-query, save-accessions case in nuccore:
julia> panda_cytb_query =
           "txid9646[ORGN:noexp] AND CYTB[GENE] " *
           "AND mitochondrion[FILT] AND 1000:1200[SLEN]";

julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/giant-panda-CYTB-candidate-accessions.txt",
           `esearch -db nuccore -query $panda_cytb_query`,
           `efetch -format acc`,
       )

julia> readlines("data/raw/giant-panda-CYTB-candidate-accessions.txt")
Do not automatically take the first returned record. Entrez result order is not a biological selection criterion.
For the full bear example, search for the more consistently annotated source: complete RefSeq mitochondrial genomes within Ursidae. Extract a small metadata table rather than downloading sequences immediately:
julia> bear_mitogenome_query =
           "txid9632[ORGN] AND mitochondrion[FILT] AND refseq[FILT] " *
           "AND \"complete genome\"[TITLE]";

julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/bear-mitogenome-candidates.tsv",
           `esearch -db nuccore -query $bear_mitogenome_query`,
           `efetch -format docsum`,
           `xtract -pattern DocumentSummary -element AccessionVersion TaxId Slen Title`,
       )

julia> open("data/raw/bear-mitogenome-candidates.tsv") do input
           for line in Iterators.take(eachline(input), 10)
               println(line)
           end
       end
Compare taxon, accession version, sequence length, title, and the detailed GenBank record. The selection below uses 1 complete mitochondrial RefSeq record for each of the 8 target species:

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect
section: 8 Save the selected accession manifest with one query
text:
8 Save the selected accession manifest with one query
Store the reviewed accession versions in Julia, construct 1 exact Entrez query, and ask NCBI to return the matching accession list:
julia> selected_accessions = [
           "NC_009492.1",
           "NC_009968.1",
           "NC_009970.1",
           "NC_009969.1",
           "NC_009971.1",
           "NC_003426.1",
           "NC_003427.1",
           "NC_003428.1",
       ];

julia> accession_query = join(
           ["$(accession)[ACCN]" for accession in selected_accessions],
           " OR ",
       );

julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/bear-mitogenome-accessions.txt",
           `esearch -db nuccore -query $accession_query`,
           `efetch -format acc`,
       )

julia> retrieved_accessions =
           readlines("data/raw/bear-mitogenome-accessions.txt");

julia> Set(retrieved_accessions) == Set(selected_accessions)
true
Save the actual query as provenance:
julia> write(
           "data/raw/bear-accession-query.txt",
           accession_query * "\n",
       );
The set comparison deliberately ignores result order but requires exactly the same unique accession versions. Do not proceed if it is false.

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect
section: 9 Fetch the reviewed records in different formats
text:
9 Fetch the reviewed records in different formats
epost reads the reviewed accession manifest once per retrieval and passes the corresponding record set to efetch. Fetch annotated GenBank flat files:
julia> accession_path = "data/raw/bear-mitogenome-accessions.txt";

julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.gb",
           `epost -db nuccore -input $accession_path`,
           `efetch -format gb`,
       )
Fetch the same whole records as FASTA:
julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.fasta",
           `epost -db nuccore -input $accession_path`,
           `efetch -format fasta`,
       )
This is the simple retrieval case: the single reviewed accession query produced 1 manifest, and epost submits that entire manifest as 1 record set.

9.1 Fetch FASTA after multiple independent queries
A more complex sampling design can require different searches for different targets. Use 3 of the reviewed bear records to practice that pattern without creating a large download:
julia> three_bear_accessions = selected_accessions[[1, 4, 8]];

julia> three_bear_paths = String[];

julia> for (index, accession) in enumerate(three_bear_accessions)
           query = "$(accession)[ACCN]"
           path = "data/raw/three-bear-accessions-$(index).txt"
           save_pipeline(
               path,
               `esearch -db nuccore -query $query`,
               `efetch -format acc`,
           )
           push!(three_bear_paths, path)
           sleep(0.4)
       end

julia> length.(readlines.(three_bear_paths))
3-element Vector{Int64}:
 1
 1
 1
Review the separate results, concatenate only the accepted accessions, and then fetch them as 1 batch:
julia> three_bear_manifest = "data/raw/three-bear-accessions.txt";

julia> concatenate_files(three_bear_paths, three_bear_manifest)

julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/three-bear-mitogenomes.fasta",
           `epost -db nuccore -input $three_bear_manifest`,
           `efetch -format fasta`,
       )

julia> count(
           line -> startswith(line, '>'),
           readlines("data/raw/three-bear-mitogenomes.fasta"),
       )
3
The individual queries could use genuinely different taxon, gene, length, or record-quality terms. Combining their reviewed accession files before epost preserves those selection boundaries while still following NCBI’s recommendation to batch the final retrieval.
The .gb file retains annotated features and source metadata. The whole-record FASTA retains headers and nucleotide strings but not the feature table. Both formats are supported by efetch; consult its sequence retrieval documentation or run efetch -help when choosing a report format.







NoteRecord source and file format are different



The selected accessions are NCBI RefSeq records. efetch -format gb serializes those records in the annotated GenBank flat-file format. “RefSeq record” names the curated record source; “GenBank format” names the representation written to the file.

Inspect the beginning of each file at the REPL:
julia> open("data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.gb") do input
           foreach(println, Iterators.take(eachline(input), 12))
       end

julia> open("data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.fasta") do input
           foreach(println, Iterators.take(eachline(input), 6))
       end


9.2 Save an accession-to-organism manifest
For machine-readable metadata, fetch INSDSeq XML with -format gbc and extract the accession version, organism, and record definition:
julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/bear-mitogenome-manifest.tsv",
           `epost -db nuccore -input $accession_path`,
           `efetch -format gbc`,
           `xtract -pattern INSDSeq -element INSDSeq_accession-version INSDSeq_organism INSDSeq_definition`,
       )

julia> print(read("data/raw/bear-mitogenome-manifest.tsv", String))
The manifest preserves the relationship between a phylogenetic tip concept and the exact sequence record used to represent it.
Record the retrieval time, software version, and discovery queries in a small provenance file:
julia> import Dates

julia> provenance = [
           "retrieved_utc\t$(Dates.now(Dates.UTC))Z",
           "edirect_version\t$(readchomp(`esearch -version`))",
           "bear_taxonomy_query\t$(bear_query)",
           "bear_mitogenome_query\t$(bear_mitogenome_query)",
       ];

julia> write(
           "data/raw/bear-retrieval-provenance.tsv",
           join(provenance, '\n') * "\n",
       );

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect
section: 10 Extract one CYTB sequence per species
text:
10 Extract one CYTB sequence per species
The whole mitochondrial FASTA file is not the intended single-locus dataset. Use the annotated CDS features in the reviewed records to extract each coding sequence. xtract -insd is the EDirect shortcut for selecting fields from INSDSeq XML; the official EDirect examples show the same CDS gene sub_sequence pattern.
Extract all annotated coding sequences to a temporary table:
julia> save_pipeline(
           "data/raw/bear-mitochondrial-cds.tsv",
           `epost -db nuccore -input $accession_path`,
           `efetch -format gbc`,
           `xtract -insd CDS gene sub_sequence`,
       )
Each row has accession version, gene name, and the nucleotide subsequence under that feature. Select CYTB case-insensitively:
julia> cds_rows = split.(
           readlines("data/raw/bear-mitochondrial-cds.tsv"),
           '\t',
       );

julia> cytb_rows = filter(cds_rows) do row
           length(row) == 3 && uppercase(row[2]) == "CYTB"
       end;

julia> length(cytb_rows)
8

julia> sequence_lengths = length.(getindex.(cytb_rows, 3))
8-element Vector{Int64}:
 1140
 1140
 1140
 1140
 1140
 1140
 1140
 1140
Validate representation and plausible full-length CYTB size before writing FASTA:
julia> @assert Set(getindex.(cytb_rows, 1)) == Set(selected_accessions)

julia> @assert all(
           sequence_length -> 1_000 <= sequence_length <= 1_200,
           sequence_lengths,
       )
Create an accession-to-organism lookup from the metadata manifest:
julia> manifest_rows = split.(
           readlines("data/raw/bear-mitogenome-manifest.tsv"),
           '\t',
       );

julia> organism_by_accession = Dict(
           row[1] => row[2] for row in manifest_rows
       );
Define a small FASTA writer that wraps sequences at 70 characters:
julia> function write_fasta_record(
           output::IO,
           identifier::AbstractString,
           sequence::AbstractString,
       )::Nothing
           println(output, ">", identifier)
           for start in firstindex(sequence):70:lastindex(sequence)
               stop = min(start + 69, lastindex(sequence))
               println(output, sequence[start:stop])
           end
           return nothing
       end

julia> raw_cytb_path = "data/raw/bears-CYTB-raw.fasta";

julia> open(raw_cytb_path, "w") do output

               organism_label = replace(organism, ' ' => '_')
               identifier = "$(organism_label)|$(accession)|CYTB"

11 Interpret the biological scope
This dataset has full terminal-taxon representation for the 8 extant bear species recognized by the explicit NCBI Taxonomy query used here. It does not therefore become a definitive species-level phylogeny.

CYTB is 1 linked mitochondrial locus, inherited as part of the mitochondrial genome.
A mitochondrial gene tree can differ from the species history because of introgression, lineage sorting, sampling, or other processes.
One database record represents each species here; it does not represent within-species variation.
Database annotations and taxonomic assignments can be revised.
The sequences must still be aligned and the alignment must be inspected.

The defensible claim at this stage is narrower: we have acquired and audited a small, consistently sourced, single-locus dataset suitable for learning the next steps in phylogenetic workflow.

2 Use EDirect pipelines
Four EDirect programs supply the operations used below:



Program
Operation




esearch
Search an Entrez database.


epost
Submit a saved list of identifiers or accessions.


efetch
Retrieve records in a specified format.


xtract
Extract fields from XML into tabular text.



The shell pipe operator | sends the output of the command on its left to the input of the command on its right. An EDirect pipeline commonly has this form:
$ esearch -db DATABASE -query 'QUERY' \
    | efetch -format xml \
    | xtract -pattern RECORD -element FIELD1 FIELD2
The continuation character \ tells the shell that the command continues on the next displayed line. The shell runs the pipeline after its final line.
The EDirect Cookbook contains additional search, fetch, and extraction recipes. The official EDirect examples document the current command options.

Post the saved accessions to nuccore and fetch the records as annotated GenBank flat files:
$ epost -db nuccore \
    -input data/raw/bear-mitogenome-accessions.txt \
    | efetch -format gb \

$ grep -c '^LOCUS' data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.gb

Inspect the records with less:
$ less data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.gb
Press q to close less. Search the flat file for CYTB gene qualifiers:
$ grep -in '/gene="cytb"' data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.gb
The selected accessions identify RefSeq records. The gb argument specifies the annotated GenBank flat-file representation. Record source and file format are separate properties.

9.1 Single-query accession set
Fetch the same posted accession set as whole-record FASTA:
$ epost -db nuccore \
    -input data/raw/bear-mitogenome-accessions.txt \
    | efetch -format fasta \
    > data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.fasta

$ grep -c '^>' data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.fasta
8

$ head data/raw/bear-mitogenomes.fasta
The GenBank file contains feature annotations and source metadata. The FASTA file contains headers and nucleotide sequences.


9.2 Multiple independent queries
Retrieve 3 reviewed accessions with 3 independent queries:
$ esearch -db nuccore -query 'NC_009492.1[ACCN]' \
    | efetch -format acc \
    > data/raw/giant-panda-mitogenome-accession.txt

$ esearch -db nuccore -query 'NC_009969.1[ACCN]' \
    | efetch -format acc \
    > data/raw/spectacled-bear-mitogenome-accession.txt

2 Run external programs from Julia
Julia’s external-program interface represents a command as a value. Julia launches the program directly; it does not place a shell between Julia and the program.

2.1 Construct a command
Backticks construct a Cmd object without running it:
julia> version_command = `esearch -version`
`esearch -version`

julia> typeof(version_command)
Cmd

julia> collect(version_command)
2-element Vector{String}:
 "esearch"
 "-version"
Each element of the command is 1 program argument.


2.2 Run a command
run starts the program and leaves its standard output connected to the terminal:
julia> run(version_command);
26.2
A command that exits with a nonzero status causes run to throw a ProcessFailedException. The success function runs a command and reports its exit status as a Boolean:
julia> success(`esearch -version`)
true


2.3 Capture standard output
read runs the program and returns its complete standard output. A terminal newline remains part of the captured string:
julia> version_text = read(version_command, String)
"26.2\n"

julia> ncodeunits(version_text)
5
readchomp removes 1 trailing line ending:
julia> edirect_version = readchomp(version_command)
"26.2"


2.4 Interpolate arguments
$ interpolates Julia values into a Cmd. A string remains 1 argument even when it contains spaces or characters that a shell would interpret:
julia> organism_name = "Ailuropoda melanoleuca"
"Ailuropoda melanoleuca"

julia> organism_query = "\"$(organism_name)\"[Scientific Name]"
"\"Ailuropoda melanoleuca\"[Scientific Name]"

julia> search_command = `esearch -db taxonomy -query $organism_query`
`esearch -db taxonomy -query '"Ailuropoda melanoleuca"[Scientific Name]'`

julia> collect(search_command)
5-element Vector{String}:
 "esearch"
 "-db"
 "taxonomy"
 "-query"
 "\"Ailuropoda melanoleuca\"[Scientific Name]"
Interpolating a collection supplies several arguments:
julia> requested_fields = ["TaxId", "ScientificName", "Rank"];

julia> field_command = `xtract -pattern Taxon -element $requested_fields`
`xtract -pattern Taxon -element TaxId ScientificName Rank`
Shell operators such as | and > do not connect or redirect programs inside Julia backticks. Julia values, IOBuffer, read, write, and pipeline provide those operations.


2.5 Supply standard input
An IOBuffer presents a Julia string as an input stream. The following pipeline call attaches that stream to the standard input of exactly 1 external program:
julia> sample_xml = """
       <Rows>
         <Row><taxon>Ursidae</taxon><rank>family</rank></Row>
         <Row><taxon>Selachii</taxon><rank>superorder</rank></Row>
       </Rows>
       """;

julia> sample_tsv = read(
           pipeline(
               `xtract -pattern Row -element taxon rank`;
               stdin = IOBuffer(sample_xml),
           ),
           String,
       )
"Ursidae\tfamily\nSelachii\tsuperorder\n"
The external program receives sample_xml through standard input. Julia captures the program’s standard output in sample_tsv.


2.6 Save and read text
write stores the captured string and returns the number of bytes written:
julia> sample_path = joinpath(raw_dir, "xtract-example.tsv")
"data/raw/xtract-example.tsv"

julia> write(sample_path, sample_tsv)
35

julia> readlines(sample_path)
2-element Vector{String}:
 "Ursidae\tfamily"
 "Selachii\tsuperorder"
open can direct a program’s standard output to a file without first materializing that output as a String:
julia> open(joinpath(raw_dir, "xtract-example-direct.tsv"), "w") do output
           run(
               pipeline(
                   `xtract -pattern Row -element taxon rank`;
                   stdin = IOBuffer(sample_xml),
                   stdout = output,
               ),
           )
       end;
This form still invokes only 1 external program.
